Preamble

This .Rmd file produces descriptive summary statistics for all variables that enter the preregistered analyses, along with several additional variables used to characterize the sample. The sections cover (i) individual-level characteristics, (ii) team-level characteristics, (iii) prior and posterior beliefs about the four hypotheses, (iv) peer evaluations of the submitted pre-analysis plans, (v) the research teams’ empirical results on the four hypotheses, (vi) the per-hypothesis and RT-level idiosyncrasy index, and (vii) the consistency between the RT-PAPs and the submitted analysis code. All descriptives are based on the research teams that completed the entire project; deviations from this sample are stated where they apply.

Individual-level characteristics

This section describes the participating researchers as individuals: team composition, recruitment channel, gender, geographic location, primary research field, academic position, publication record, and self-rated experience. All counts and frequencies refer to individual researchers (rather than research teams).

[Team composition] Our sample comprises 230 individual researchers, organized in 127 research teams who completed all project stages: 103 teams consist of two members, and 24 teams include only one member.

[Recruitment channels] Of the researchers involved, 43 (18.7%) learned about the study via Lab² announcements, 24 (10.4%) via SOEP announcements, 27 (11.7%) through one of the research coordinators, and 74 (32.2%) through their research team member. 62 (27%) researchers reported having learned about the study through other channels.

[Gender] Of the 230 individual researchers involved as research team members, 77 (33.5%) identify as female and 151 (65.7%) identify as male; 2 (0.9%) classify themselves as “other.”

[Location] The vast majority of participants are from Europe (\(n\) = 194; 84.3%), followed by Northern America (\(n\) = 17; 7.4%), Asia (\(n\) = 13; 5.7%), Latin America (\(n\) = 3; 1.3%), and Oceania (\(n\) = 3; 1.3%).

[Research field] Most participants (\(n\) = 148; 64.3%) report Economics as their primary field of research, followed by Sociology (\(n\) = 40; 17.4%), Business Administration (\(n\) = 14; 6.1%), Finance (\(n\) = 11; 4.8%), Political Science (\(n\) = 9; 3.9%), Psychology (\(n\) = 4; 1.7%), and other fields (\(n\) = 4; 1.7%).

[Position] Among the 230 researchers involved, 24 (10.4%) are full professors, 25 (10.9%) are associate professors, 54 (23.5%) are assistant professors, 77 (33.5%) are post-doctoral researchers, and 34 (14.8%) are PhD candidates. The remaining participants hold other positions within or beyond academia.

[Publications] Of the 230 individual researchers, 81 (35.2%) have published at least one article in a top-tier journal (_AJG 4*_ according to the ABS rating, or included in the FT50 journal list). While 215 (93.5%) researchers have at least one publication employing empirical methods, only 50 (21.7%) have published work related to a study on the “daughters” hypothesis.

[Experience] The table below summarizes participants’ self-rated experience (rated on scales from 0 [“no experience”] to 10 [“extensive experience”]) in regression analysis, Stata, large datasets, and pre-analysis plans. Among the 230 researchers involved, 91 (39.6%) had previously participated in a meta-scientific crowd-science project, and 84 (36.5%) had used SOEP data before.

Team-level characteristics

This section describes the research teams. The first paragraph summarizes team composition (size, seniority, field affiliation, top-tier publication record, and prior SOEP experience), using the team-level aggregations defined in PAP §2.2. The table that follows reports the teams’ self-reported effort (+), modeling approach (§), and aggregated experience (#).

[Team composition] Of the 160 research teams recruited into the project, 33 dropped out before completion (PAP §3), leaving 127 teams that completed all project stages and constitute our sample. 103 (81.1%) teams consist of two members; 24 (18.9%) teams include only one member. Of the participating teams, 41 (32.3%) included at least one senior researcher (full or associate professor), 95 (74.8%) had at least one member affiliated with economics or finance, 66 (52%) included a member with a top-tier publication, and 60 (47.2%) included a member experienced in using SOEP data.

[Effort, approach, experience] The table below presents team-level measures of research teams’ self-reported effort (+), their approach to developing the analytical model (§), and their self-rated experience (#). The number of iterations to computational reproducibility was tracked by the project coordinators; effort, hours spent, and the modeling-approach items were reported jointly by each team in the post-Stage 2 survey. Experience-related variables are derived from individual-level survey responses and aggregated to the team level using the maximum across team members; “Experience: Analysis” is the average of researchers’ reported experience with (i) regression analysis, (ii) Stata, and (iii) large datasets. Two teams (one per condition) reported more than 600 hours — far above the rest of the distribution — so the table additionally reports hours worked after excluding these two outliers.

Balance across treatment conditions

Research teams were randomized into the two conditions when they entered the project — before any team received data, and before the Survey #1 belief elicitation. The table below compares the two conditions on the team-level characteristics that enter the preregistered analyses as controls (PAP §2.2) and on the prior beliefs elicited in Survey #1, across the research teams that completed the project.

The \(p\)-values are descriptive: they summarize how far apart the two conditions happen to be on each characteristic in the realized sample, and no inference is drawn from them. They are unadjusted, and eleven comparisons are reported, so isolated values below conventional thresholds are expected even under perfectly balanced randomization.

Peer evaluations

This section summarizes the peer evaluations of the submitted RT-PAPs. Each completing RT rated ten anonymized RT-PAPs (five per group, excluding its own) on (i) the reasonableness of the proposed analysis and (ii) the informativeness of the pre-analysis plan, both on a 0-10 scale, separately for each of the four hypotheses; the per-rating PAP quality is the mean of the two scores (PAP §2.1).

The table reports descriptive statistics for the raw scores and for the corresponding rater-demeaned scores (each rating minus the rater’s mean rating for that hypothesis), the latter implicitly netting out rater fixed effects. Each statistic is computed across the per-(rated team \(\times\) hypothesis) mean ratings — the individual ratings are first averaged over the (approximately ten) raters of each PAP — so the reported standard deviations are between-PAP standard deviations of the mean rating, smaller than the standard deviations of the individual ratings by roughly \(\sqrt{10}\) (the individual-rating SDs are reported in the table note below). Demeaning here is for descriptive comparability only; the preregistered tests in PAP §3.2.2 use the individual ratings together with rater fixed effects.

Research teams’ results

This section summarizes the research teams’ empirical estimates for the four hypotheses, restricted to teams that submitted valid estimates for all four. 7 teams produced analyses that yielded improper statistical estimates (e.g., standard errors equal to zero) for at least one of the four hypotheses; these teams are excluded here, as in all results-based analyses (an exclusion that is not preregistered). Consequently, the descriptive statistics below are based on a sample of \(n\) = 120 teams.

The first table summarizes the standardized \(z\)-values and absolute deviations by hypothesis. Positive \(z\)-values indicate estimates consistent with the hypothesized effects, whereas negative \(z\)-values correspond to estimates in the opposite direction. Absolute deviations are computed relative to the group-specific mean of \(z\); the table pools observations across groups.

Idiosyncrasy index

Following the pre-analysis plan (§2.1), the idiosyncrasy index for research team \(i\) and RT Hypothesis \(h\) is defined as \(I_{i,h} = 1 - F_{i,h}(D_5)\), where \(F_{i,h}\) denotes the empirical cumulative distribution of \(p\)-values obtained by applying RT \(i\)’s analysis code to placebo 5%-subsamples of the SOEP data and \(D_5\) denotes the original 5%-sample. Higher values indicate that the team’s \(p\)-value on the original 5%-sample is unusually small relative to the placebo distribution, suggestive of an idiosyncratic (“lucky”) result on the original 5%-sample. The RT idiosyncrasy index aggregates the per-hypothesis indices to the team level as \(I_i = \frac{1}{4} \sum_{h=1}^{4} I_{i,h}\).

The pre-analysis plan specifies 1,000 placebo subsamples per (RT \(\times\) hypothesis) cell. That target is met for 409 of the 479 cells with a non-missing index; the remaining 70 cells rest on fewer draws (median 970, minimum 31), because some teams’ analysis code did not execute on every subsample. Cells resting on fewer draws estimate \(F_{i,h}\) more coarsely, which makes the index granular rather than biased.

The table below reports how the usable iterations are distributed, by hypothesis and treatment condition: the number of cells with a non-missing index, how many of them reach the registered target of 1,000 placebo draws, and the smallest realized number of draws. Completion is comparable across the two conditions in every hypothesis. Restricting the tests that use the index (Secondary hypotheses 7 to 9) to the cells that reach 1,000 draws leaves the conclusions unchanged; those restricted estimates are reported in 03_preregistered_analyses.Rmd.

RT-PAP / code consistency

Following PAP §1.5, the project coordinators audited the consistency between each RT’s pre-analysis plan and its submitted Stata code. A random 10% of RT-PAPs was checked first; because the inconsistency rate in that random sample exceeded the 20% escalation threshold, all RT-PAP/code pairs were subsequently reviewed. Deviating from the per-hypothesis indicator described in PAP §2.1, consistency was recorded as a single overall verdict per RT, together with the number and type of deviations of the code from the PAP. All statistics below are based on the 127 research teams that completed the project.

[Audit and escalation] The random 10% audit covered 14 RT-PAP/code pairs, of which 7 (50%) were judged inconsistent. As this exceeds the 20% escalation threshold (PAP §1.5), all 127 completed RT-PAP/code pairs were reviewed; 47 (37%) were found inconsistent overall.

Across the 47 inconsistent pairs, the auditors recorded 163 individual deviations of the code from the PAP — a mean of 3.5 per inconsistent pair (median 4, maximum 15). A further 4 pairs contained isolated deviations the auditors judged immaterial and classified as consistent; these are excluded from the category and severity counts below.

The tables below report, in turn: (i) the number and share of inconsistent pairs, pooled and by treatment condition; (ii) the breakdown of the recorded deviations by category, among the inconsistent pairs (the number of pairs affected, their share of all inconsistent pairs, and the total number of occurrences), pooled and separately by treatment condition; and (iii) the number of deviations per inconsistent pair, by treatment condition. Where the code’s sample filters or control sets departed from the PAP, the deviations more often involved stricter filters and fewer controls than specified, rather than the reverse. The two conditions contribute different numbers of inconsistent pairs, so the per-condition counts in the second table are not directly comparable; the denominators are given in the column headers.
